newsitem.title: DUBAI: Dubai's Emirates Group profits up 35 percent.
newsitem.headline: Dubai's Emirates Group profits up 35 percent.

text.p: The Dubai government-owned Emirates Group reported profits of 194.2 million dirhams ($52.9 million) for the 1996/7 financial year, a 35 percent increase on the 143.7 million dirhams posted in the year to end-March 1996.
Overall revenues climbed 17 percent to some $1 billion.

"It has not been an easy year...when other travel companies are reporting reduced profits or losses, we are once again firmly in the black," said chairman Sheikh Ahmed bin Saeed al-Maktoum at a news conference on Sunday.
The group, made up of Emirates airline and Dubai airport handler and travel management company DNATA, said it was targeting 260 million dirhams profit for the financial year ending in March 1998.
A statement by the group said the airline division posted profit of 111.5 million dirhams and DNATA had an 82.7 million dirhams profit, increases of 38 and 31 percent respectively.
It said the 12 year-old airline carried three million passengers and 159,000 tonnes of freight in the year, with an overall load factor of 69 percent.
Sheikh Ahmed said airline yields declined to 59 U.S. cents per revenue tonne km from 63 cents, while rising jet fuel costs added $13.6 million to the group's operating expenses.
But lower yields were offset by 40 million dirham cost cutting plan and a 6.5 percent reduction in unit costs per available tonne km to 39 cents from 41 cents.
Cargo volumes rose 23 percent on the previous year resulting in increase in cargo's contribution to revenue to 17 percent.
Sheikh Ahmed said DNATA would pay 25 million dirhams of profit to the Dubai government and the airline would retain its full profit.

Group managing director Maurice Flanagan said the airline was not considering buying all-cargo freighter aircraft. "We are doing well in the freight business and we have no plans to go under the burden of buying freighters."
In the 1996/97 financial year Emirates had a fleet of 19 aircraft with an average age of 61 months flying to 41 cities.
The group's financial director Dermot Mannion said the airline's long-term liabilities were 2.2 billion dirhams.

Emirates in November signed deals with Airbus Industrie for 16 new A330-200 aircraft with delivery starting in January 1999, and for the purchase of 36 Rolls-Royce Trent 772 engines. The deals are worth more than $2 billion.
